Remember that our central argument is the physically motivated postulate (P4). In order to show how
our construction guarantees the local action of operators, consider the tensor product of two operators of
the form given in Eq. (4): Tensor products IFa ⊗IFb, IFa ⊗JFb, JFa ⊗IFb, and JFa ⊗JFb of the flag operators
appear. As can be easily seen, IFa ⊗IFb and −JFa ⊗JFb act as the identity operator IF on the basis states
(equivalence classes) |0⟩⟩F and |1⟩⟩F , see Eq. (7), of the flag of the composite system. Analogously, IFa ⊗JFb
and JFa ⊗IFb act as JF on these basis states (see also Eq. (59)).2 Hence, the embedding of the local actions
on subsystems into the operators for the composite system is well-defined. The postulate of local action
(P4) is satisfied because the underlying structure is still the tensor product of the Hilbert spaces, though
with an additional equivalence relation. (The satisfaction of (P4) in real and complex quantum mechanics
is analyzed in more detail in Section E of the Supplementary Material.) The reduced density operator in
the real-valued formalism is still given via the (real) partial trace, which is derived in Section F of the
Supplementary Material.
In summary, we propose a formulation of quantum mechanics based on real numbers, which leads to
exactly the same predictions for experimental outcomes as standard complex quantum mechanics (see Eq. (6)
and discussion below). Recent literature [12, 14, 15, 16] based their arguments on the mathematical postulate
of a tensor product structure for the real description of composite quantum systems. We show, however, that
the theory resulting from that postulate does not correspond to standard quantum mechanics, as it fails to
capture the ambiguity in assigning the global phase of a product state to its subsystems [17, 18, 19, 20].
Instead, we argue that a postulate based on physical properties for composite systems – namely that a
local operation on one subsystem acts trivially on the other – is well motivated and does lead to a theory
that corresponds to standard quantum mechanics. The above-mentioned phase ambiguity is ensured by
employing the quotient space of the real tensor product. We show that our construction fulfills the required
physical postulate and is unique (up to isomorphisms). Note that a similar real representation has been
discussed in the literature before [7, 8, 9, 10] – however, there it was not considered to be equivalent to
standard quantum theory. We mention that a tensor product in standard complex quantum mechanics can
also be formulated as a quotient space [22, 23] and fulfills our physically motivated postulate. In conclusion,
complex numbers are not necessary to describe quantum mechanics – but they are certainly very useful.
